Newborn Care

Stickler syndrome: causes, signs and ongoing care

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Stickler syndrome can affect several parts of the body, especially the eyes, hearing and joints. It is often recognized in infancy or childhood, but the combination and severity of features differ, even within a family. Early assessment helps identify the problems that need attention before they interfere with a child’s sight, communication or everyday activities.

What Stickler syndrome is

Stickler syndrome is a group of genetic connective-tissue conditions. Connective tissue provides support and structure in many parts of the body. An older medical name is hereditary progressive arthro-ophthalmopathy, referring to its joint and eye features.

Some children have a flatter middle part of the face, a small nose or a small, recessed lower jaw. The eyes may look prominent. A cleft palate, an opening in the roof of the mouth, can also be present. None of these features alone confirms the condition.

One child may have obvious problems early, while a relative has much subtler signs. Looking at the eyes, hearing, joints and family history together is more useful than expecting every child to match a single description.

Eye changes and the importance of retinal care

Marked short-sightedness, or myopia, can appear early. The vitreous, the clear gel within the eye, may develop differently. Cataracts, which cloud the lens, and glaucoma, which involves damage to the optic nerve often associated with raised eye pressure, are other possible concerns.

Some forms carry a substantial risk of retinal tears or detachment. The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. If it separates, vision can be permanently damaged, making prompt eye assessment especially important.

Ask for care from an ophthalmologist familiar with inherited vitreous and retinal disorders. The risk depends on the type of Stickler syndrome and the findings in the individual eye; the same warning should not be interpreted as the same probability for everyone.

A retina specialist may discuss preventive laser or freezing treatment in suitable cases. This is different from repairing a detachment that has already happened. Preventive treatment can reduce risk but cannot promise that a detachment will never occur.

New flashes, a sudden increase in floaters, a dark shadow or curtain, or sudden blurred vision need urgent assessment. Do not wait for an annual appointment. Young children may not describe these changes, so keep scheduled examinations and ask the team how to respond to any new concern about visual behaviour.

Hearing and ear problems

Hearing loss can be mild or more marked and may change over time. Difficulty hearing higher-pitched sounds can occur, but the pattern is not identical in every person. Both inner-ear hearing loss and problems conducting sound through the middle ear are possible.

Children with cleft palate or related facial differences can also have repeated middle-ear problems. A child who seems not to listen, struggles with speech sounds or changes how they respond to voices needs assessment rather than being assumed to be inattentive.

An audiologist and ENT team can identify the type of difficulty and discuss support. Depending on the findings, care may include hearing devices, treatment of ear disease or other measures to improve access to sound. Hearing loss does not inevitably progress to complete deafness.

Joints, spine and dental development

Children may have very flexible joints. Pain, stiffness or degenerative joint changes can develop unusually early, sometimes in adolescence or young adulthood, but arthritis is not guaranteed to begin at one particular age.

An abnormal curve in the spine, such as scoliosis or kyphosis, can cause additional problems. Report persistent pain, changes in movement or difficulty taking part in normal activities so that the child can receive an appropriate musculoskeletal assessment.

A smaller jaw can leave less room for teeth and contribute to crowding or an uneven bite. Dental and orthodontic review can help plan care as adult teeth develop. Braces or surgery may be considered when needed; not every child needs the same intervention.

Collagen genes and family risk

Many forms result from changes in genes involved in making collagen. Collagen gives connective tissue strength and structure, including in joint cartilage and parts of the eye. Different gene changes help explain why the pattern varies.

The common forms are autosomal dominant: one altered copy of the relevant gene can cause the condition. For someone with a dominant form, each pregnancy carries a 50% chance of passing on the variant. A new genetic change can also occur without a known family history.

Rarer forms are autosomal recessive. When both parents carry a disease-causing change in the same relevant gene, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of an affected child. These are different inheritance situations, so a vague statement that family risk is simply high is not enough.

A genetics professional can explain the result for your family and whether relatives need assessment. Having a relative with mild signs does not guarantee that another affected person will have the same experience.

Feeding and breathing in infancy

A small lower jaw, a tongue positioned farther back and a cleft palate can occur together as Pierre Robin sequence. In a newborn, this combination can interfere with breathing or feeding and deserves early specialist attention.

The baby may need coordinated airway, cleft-palate and feeding care. The team can assess milk transfer, growth and breathing and recommend equipment or treatment for that baby. Significant airway obstruction sometimes needs surgery or other specialist support.

Do not try to solve breathing problems by changing the baby’s sleep position or adding pillows without a prescribed medical plan. Severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, or difficulty waking requires emergency help. A baby who struggles to feed needs prompt advice even when they seem settled between feeds.

Diagnosis and a follow-up plan

Assessment combines clinical findings, family history and, when appropriate, genetic testing. Eye and hearing examinations can reveal issues that are not obvious from the child’s appearance. Identifying the subtype helps make the surveillance plan more specific.

GeneReviews recommends annual review by a vitreoretinal specialist and annual audiology assessment as a general framework. Younger children, existing hearing problems or other findings can justify more frequent appointments. Your child’s team should set the actual schedule.

Keep a written plan for the next eye and hearing checks, musculoskeletal review when needed, and dental or craniofacial follow-up. A normal check is useful information, but it does not cancel future surveillance or mean new symptoms should wait.

How to understand the heart-valve question

Older reports suggested an increased rate of mitral valve prolapse, a condition affecting a heart valve. Later research in a genetically confirmed group did not find that increased rate. The evidence does not justify telling every family that heart-valve disease is an expected feature.

This does not mean heart symptoms or an abnormal examination should be ignored. The clinician can decide whether cardiac assessment is indicated for the individual. Do not arrange or reject tests, or start preventive antibiotics, solely on the basis of a general description of Stickler syndrome.

Treatment can reduce complications

There is no single cure that removes the underlying genetic condition. Treatment can nevertheless correct specific problems, preserve function and reduce the chance of serious complications.

Care may include glasses or eye procedures, hearing support, treatment of ear infections, help for joint pain and movement, dental treatment, or surgery for a cleft palate, jaw or other structural difficulty. The priorities depend on the child, not on completing every treatment on a list.

Ask the team which concerns are urgent, which are being monitored and what changes should trigger a call. School accommodations and communication support can be important alongside medical care. The goal is to protect health and participation while keeping the plan understandable for the family.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The eye, hearing, joint and craniofacial pattern varies by person and genetic subtype.

Regular retinal and hearing surveillance is important, with frequency individualized.

Retinal-detachment symptoms require urgent assessment even between normal routine checks.

How BeMama can help

Keep a simple follow-up list and an urgent eye-contact plan. Ask how the confirmed subtype changes the care your child needs.

When to seek help

Sudden changes in vision and significant newborn breathing or feeding problems need prompt assessment. General information cannot replace the child’s specialist surveillance plan.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Stickler syndrome can affect eyes, hearing, joints and facial development in different combinations.
  • Inheritance may be dominant, recessive or due to a new variant.
  • Do not wait for a routine eye visit if vision changes suddenly.
  • Treatment helps manage problems even though there is no single genetic cure.

Frequently asked questions

Does having an affected parent increase the chance of Stickler syndrome?

Yes, but the exact chance depends on the genetic form. A parent with a dominant form has a 50% chance in each pregnancy of passing on the variant. A genetics professional can explain other situations.

What signs should families know about?

Possible features include marked short-sightedness, retinal problems, hearing loss, flexible or painful joints and a small jaw or cleft palate. The combination and severity vary.

What causes Stickler syndrome?

Many forms involve changes in collagen-related genes. Collagen helps support connective tissue in structures such as joints and the eye.

Can Stickler syndrome be treated?

Yes. Although there is no single cure for the genetic condition, eye care, hearing support, joint treatment and selected operations can manage symptoms and reduce complications.

How often should my child’s hearing be checked?

Annual audiology is a general surveillance framework, but young children or those with hearing and ear problems may need more frequent checks. Follow the individual plan.

Which eye symptoms need urgent help?

New flashes, sudden floaters, a shadow or curtain, or sudden blurred vision need urgent assessment. Do not wait for the next planned appointment.

Does every child develop arthritis in adolescence?

No. Joint problems can begin early, but timing and severity vary. Pain or reduced movement should be assessed rather than treated as an inevitable milestone.

Are heart-valve problems inevitable?

No. Historical reports have differed, and a genetically confirmed study did not support a blanket increased-risk claim. Cardiac testing should follow the person’s findings and clinical advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
